Religion, Revolution, and Terror: Iran 1979 to 9/11

Mini-lesson · Mr. Magister

From Tehran to September 11

11951 to 1977: the Shah and the coup of 1953
21978 to 1979: protests and the Islamic Republic
31979 to 1988: the hostages and the war with Iraq

5September 11, 2001
Today's Focus

How did a revolution in Iran, a war in Afghanistan, and a network of extremists lead to the attacks of September 11?

Just as the Cold War was ending, a different kind of struggle was taking shape in the Middle East and Central Asia. Today you will see how a revolution in Iran, a war in Afghanistan, and a network of violent extremists led to the attacks of September 11, 2001.

Objectives
  1. Explain how the Iranian Revolution of 1979 replaced a monarchy with a government led by religious authorities.
  2. Describe how the war in Afghanistan helped give rise to al-Qaeda and the Taliban.
  3. Describe the attacks of September 11, 2001, and the choices that led to them.
Quick Check-in

Just as the Cold War was ending, a different kind of struggle was taking shape in the Middle East and Central Asia. Before you read: what do you expect connected the events that led to September 11, 2001?

Religion, Revolution, and Terror: Iran 1979 to 9/11

Part 1

Iran and the Shah

Chapter 1Iran and the Shah
Chapter 1

Iran and the Shah

Iran, an ancient country of Persian culture, was ruled in the twentieth century by the Pahlavi family. Its oil was developed by a British company, and many Iranians resented that foreigners took the profits. In 1951 the prime minister, Mohammad Mossadegh, nationalized the oil industry. Britain and the United States, fearing that Iran might drift toward the Soviet side, helped organize a coup in 1953 that removed him and restored the young Shah, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, to full power.

Mossadegh was a lawyer and a nationalist, and his oil law was popular. Britain answered with a boycott that choked Iran's income. In August 1953 the American CIA and the British secret service backed a plot against him. The first attempt failed, and the Shah, who had signed the order dismissing Mossadegh, fled the country for Rome. Days later crowds, some of them paid by the plotters, and soldiers loyal to the Shah turned the tables, and Mossadegh was arrested. The Shah came home and ruled with American backing for more than twenty-five years. Many Iranians never forgot that a government they had chosen was removed from outside.

The Shah ruled as a modernizer. In the 1960s his "White Revolution" gave land to peasants, gave women the vote, and built schools and factories. But he ruled as an autocrat, banned real opposition, and relied on a secret police called SAVAK. Oil money flowed in, and the gap between the wealthy and the poor grew. Many religious Iranians were angered by his Western ways, and many bazaar merchants and students resented his power. His alliance with America made the United States a target of their anger.

In 1971 the Shah held a great celebration at the ruins of Persepolis to mark twenty-five hundred years of Persian monarchy, with guests from around the world, while many Iranians went without. After 1973, when oil prices quadrupled, Iran's income soared and the Shah spent it on armies, factories, and show. Millions of villagers moved to the cities, where jobs, housing, and wages could not keep up with prices. There was no free press or open party through which their anger could be heard.

Part 2

The Revolution of 1979

Chapter 2The Revolution of 1979
Chapter 2

The Revolution of 1979

Most Iranians belong to the Shia branch of Islam, which differs from the Sunni branch, to which most Muslims elsewhere belong, over who should lead the community after Muhammad. Shia clergy have long held great moral authority. The Shah's chief critic was an ayatollah, Ruhollah Khomeini, who denounced him for corruption and for submission to the West. Khomeini was exiled in 1964 and spent years in Iraq and then France, where his sermons were smuggled home on cassette tapes.

The spark came in January 1978, when a newspaper printed an article insulting Khomeini. Students and clerics protested in the holy city of Qom, and police killed some of them. Shia custom marks a death with mourning forty days later, and so each memorial became a new protest, with new deaths and another forty days to come. By September the pattern had spread across the country. On September 8 soldiers fired on a crowd in Tehran's Jaleh Square, and Iranians called the day Black Friday. After that, many who had hoped for a compromise with the Shah gave up on him.

In 1978 protests began, and when soldiers fired on crowds the protests grew. Strikes, including those of oil workers, paralyzed the country. The Shah, secretly ill with cancer, hesitated to use full force, and some of his generals lost heart. He left Iran in January 1979. Khomeini returned in triumph in February, and a referendum soon created an Islamic Republic. Khomeini taught that, in the absence of the hidden Imam, the senior scholars should rule. The result was a theocracy, with an elected president and parliament but a Supreme Leader above them. Many who had joined the revolution, including liberals and the left, found themselves jailed or silenced. The Shah's fall was not inevitable. A different response in 1978 might have kept him on the throne.

In the first months of the republic, revolutionary courts executed hundreds of officials of the old regime. The first prime minister, a moderate, resigned in November after the embassy was seized. In December 1979 a new constitution, approved by a vote, placed the Supreme Leader above the elected offices, with power over the armed forces and the courts.

Part 3

Hostages and War

Chapter 3Hostages and War
Chapter 3

Hostages and War

In October 1979 President Jimmy Carter allowed the exiled Shah to enter the United States for medical treatment. Many Iranians feared a repeat of 1953. On November 4, students stormed the American embassy in Tehran and seized more than sixty Americans. Khomeini backed them. Fifty-two of the hostages were held for 444 days, released only on the day Ronald Reagan took office in January 1981. An American rescue attempt failed in the desert. The crisis humiliated the United States and helped to defeat Carter's bid for re-election.

The rescue attempt came in April 1980. Helicopters flew from an aircraft carrier to a remote place in the Iranian desert, but several broke down or were blinded by a sandstorm, and the commander called off the mission. In the dark a helicopter collided with a transport plane, and eight American servicemen died. The Iranian government displayed the wreckage. The hostages were scattered among other cities, and they were freed after long talks through Algeria, minutes after Reagan took the oath of office.

In September 1980 Iraq's dictator, Saddam Hussein, invaded Iran, expecting a quick victory over a country in turmoil. Instead the war lasted eight years and killed hundreds of thousands. Iran used waves of young volunteers, and Iraq used poison gas, against Iran and against its own Kurdish citizens. Both sides were exhausted by the end in 1988, with the borders where they started. Khomeini died in 1989, and his system outlived him.

Iraq's army crossed the border on September 22, 1980. It took the port city of Khorramshahr after weeks of street fighting, but Iran retook it in 1982 and then carried the war into Iraq. Khomeini refused to end the fighting while Saddam remained in power. Boys in their early teens were among the volunteers sent against Iraqi machine guns, and the cities of both countries came under missile attack. In March 1988 Iraqi planes dropped poison gas on the Kurdish town of Halabja and killed thousands of civilians. When Khomeini finally accepted a cease-fire that summer, he said that it was like drinking poison.

Part 4

Afghanistan and al-Qaeda

Chapter 4Afghanistan and al-Qaeda
Chapter 4

Afghanistan and al-Qaeda

In December 1979 Soviet troops invaded Afghanistan to prop up a communist government. Many Afghans, a deeply religious and tribal people, rose against it. These fighters, the mujahideen, received weapons and money from the United States, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan, and many volunteers came from other Muslim lands. A wealthy young Saudi named Osama bin Laden helped to fund and organize some of them. The Soviets withdrew in 1989 after nearly ten years, a defeat that helped bring on the collapse of the Soviet Union.

The Soviet army had expected a short campaign. Instead it faced guerrillas who knew the mountains and could retreat across the border into Pakistan, where millions of Afghan refugees found shelter. In 1986 the United States began to supply the mujahideen with Stinger missiles, which made Soviet helicopters vulnerable. About fifteen thousand Soviet soldiers died. Afghans died in far greater numbers, perhaps a million or more, and millions more were driven abroad as refugees. The Soviet leader, Mikhail Gorbachev, who wanted out of the war, brought the last troops home in February 1989.

When the Soviets left, the world lost interest, and Afghanistan fell into civil war. A movement of religious students, the Taliban, took the capital, Kabul, in 1996, and imposed a harsh rule, forbidding girls to attend school and barring women from most work. Bin Laden, who had turned against the United States, formed a network called al-Qaeda, meaning "the base." He had objected to American troops in Saudi Arabia, home to Islam's holiest cities, after the Gulf War of 1991, and he issued a declaration of war on Americans in 1996. The Taliban gave him a base.

Bin Laden had spent the early 1990s in Sudan and returned to Afghanistan in 1996 after the Sudanese government expelled him. The Taliban had risen in 1994 around the southern city of Kandahar under a cleric named Mullah Omar, and by the time they held Kabul they ruled most of the country. In 1998 bin Laden and his allies announced that Muslims should kill Americans, soldiers and civilians alike, anywhere in the world. In March 2001 the Taliban blew up two huge Buddha statues carved into a cliff at Bamiyan some fifteen hundred years earlier, over protests from governments and scholars across the world.

Al-Qaeda practiced terrorism. In 1993 a bomb exploded beneath the World Trade Center in New York, killing six. In August 1998 truck bombs destroyed the American embassies in Kenya and Tanzania, killing more than two hundred people, most of them Africans. In October 2000 a small boat packed with explosives hit the destroyer USS Cole in Yemen and killed seventeen sailors. Most Muslims, including most religious scholars, rejected such violence, and most victims of the extremists were themselves Muslims.

Part 5

September 11, 2001

Chapter 5September 11, 2001
Chapter 5

September 11, 2001

On the morning of September 11, 2001, nineteen men, most of them from Saudi Arabia, boarded four airliners in the northeastern United States. Armed with box cutters, they took over the planes. At 8:46 one flew into the north tower of the World Trade Center, and at 9:03 another struck the south tower. At 9:37 a third hit the Pentagon, near Washington. Passengers on the fourth, Flight 93, learned by telephone what had happened to the others. They fought the hijackers, and the plane crashed in a field in Pennsylvania, short of its target, which was probably the Capitol or the White House. Both towers collapsed within two hours.

The hijackers had studied the system as much as the aircraft. Their flights from Boston, Newark, and Washington were bound for California, so the planes carried heavy loads of fuel. Federal rules then allowed passengers to carry small knives, and airline crews had been trained to cooperate with hijackers and land the plane, because in earlier hijackings the men had wanted money or a flight to another country. No one in charge had imagined airliners used as missiles. Flight 93 left Newark late, so its passengers had time to learn what was happening before the hijackers took control. They decided to rush the cockpit, and one of them, Todd Beamer, was heard on an open telephone line saying, "Let's roll." At the Pentagon 184 people died, counting those aboard the plane, and the final toll across the three sites was 2,977, not counting the hijackers.

Nearly three thousand people from more than ninety countries died, the deadliest attack on American soil. Firefighters and police climbed the stairs as others fled, and 343 firefighters were among the dead. Air travel in the United States halted for days. It was a day of horror, and also of courage, as many ordinary people helped strangers.

The president was reading to schoolchildren in Florida when an aide whispered the news, and he spent the day flying between air bases while the country wondered whether more attacks were coming. On September 14 he stood on the wreckage at the World Trade Center with a bullhorn and told the crowd that the rest of the world heard them and that the people who had knocked the buildings down would hear from all of them soon. America's allies in NATO, for the first time in the alliance's history, invoked the clause that treats an attack on one member as an attack on all.

President George W. Bush spoke to Congress on September 20, which you will read. He said that the United States would hold responsible any nation that harbored terrorists, and in October American and allied forces, with Afghan allies, began a war that drove the Taliban from power. Bin Laden slipped away in the mountains of Tora Bora that December. In the next lesson you will see the wider world that these events shook.
